Um... to me most scientists are following a particular axiomatic system called Epicurianism. There are assumptions that most scientists make independent of the scientific method, which is a very pure system. Those are materialism, that physical things are the only substantial things in the universe, and the small scale indivisibility of matter itself.

I'm of the mind that Cartesian ideas should be thought about more by scientists before they so willingly embrace pure materialism and validity of atomicity. On atomicity, we have gone through the chemical elements, which we still call atoms, but have managed to split them into nucleus and electron. We obviously split the nucleus into hadrons, and now we split hadrons into quarks. We have also split the electron into spinons and some other interesting stuff. At every level, there were implicit assumptions that we had finally hit bottom. Their track record makes me skeptical.

On materialism, I can't help but think that given our experience of abstract things like numbers and the qualia of, say, colors, is substantially different from all of our models of objective reality, and so I think that they are substantially different. Our models provide symbols that we can associate with these experiences, but the symbol 'red' will not describe what red looks like to someone that has never seen it.

But perhaps I am wrong and consciousness is generated by matter interactions.

Back to the original question: Just because your religion of Epicurianism is very, very, useful doesn't mean it gives answers to really important human questions. Once all that there is in your universe is matter, humans are just a very complex collection of it. Nothing particularly special about them. So it is hard to derive things like natural rights for things that aren't substantially different from, say, chairs. Just arbitrarily naming human rights doesn't seem to convince most people as to their validity, and so implementing them becomes a problem. So, then, I find myself obliged to desire something that is more important than just matter. And, in fact, I am a thinking, feeling being with a consciousness. The fact that we are here, all of us, in what is essentially a one in an infinity of probability, is amazing. And we can perceive metaphysical things like happiness and pain. We perceive value. I cannot point to anything else in the world that doesn't have consciousness that perceives value. And so, we are the ones that determine value. Our consciousness sets up value. And that's why it is different and needs more thought.

I guess that's more of a philosophy than a religion, but quoting a god while telling people they should kill, rape and steal is just a shortcut to me. Of course, religion often gets out of hand, and I think we should, equipped with knowledge that our consciousness is necessary for things of value to exist, keep things rational.
